analysis.one_liner: Bans importation of goods made abroad by child labor.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a vote, never leaving committee before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Labor Department to identify foreign industries that use children under 15 to make exported goods, and then barred those goods from entering the United States, with civil and criminal penalties for importers. It also urged the President to seek an international agreement banning trade in products of child labor. It was introduced in October 1992 with no cosponsors and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which sent it to its Trade Subcommittee; nothing further happened before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, children abroad who are put to work making exported goods would have faced a lost market for that labor, adult workers in exporting countries would have faced less competition from underage workers, and U.S. workers would have faced less job pressure from imports made with child labor. Consumers would have gained a certification system showing that imported goods were not made with child labor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in export industries and adult workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibited the entry of any manufactured article produced by a foreign industry identified as using child labor, with an exception only if the importer certified it took reasonable steps to ensure the article was not a product of child labor [S3].

It created a process, open to petitions from any person, for the Secretary of Labor to identify foreign industries and host countries that use child labor in exported products, with findings published in the Federal Register [S2][S3].

It set civil penalties up to $25,000 and criminal penalties including fines and up to one year of imprisonment for knowingly importing covered goods, and treated violations as customs-law violations subject to search, seizure, and forfeiture [S3].

The bill's stated purpose was to eliminate the United States' role as a market for products made by children under 15 and to press other nations to join an international trade ban, citing International Labor Organization estimates that 200 million children under 15 were working worldwide [S3].

Its findings declared that U.S. and other developed-country workers should not have their jobs imperiled by imports produced with child labor, and that child employment denies jobs to millions of adults [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Importers and retailers of labor-intensive goods such as apparel, carpets, and minerals would have borne the cost of certification, the risk of seizure at the border, and penalties up to $25,000 per violation plus criminal exposure. Consumers could have paid somewhat higher prices for goods stripped of child labor from their supply chains. Foreign industries relying on child labor would have lost U.S. sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: Importers and retailers of consumer goods

drawbacks.text: The bill required importers to document that their purchase agreements barred child labor, adding paperwork and supply-chain compliance costs, and its definitions reach any product containing any part made by a child, including crude minerals — a broad net that could sweep in many goods [S3].

A good-faith objection to import bans of this kind is that cutting off export work can push children into less visible, less regulated sectors rather than into school; a ban targets the symptom in export industries while leaving domestic child labor untouched, which honest supporters would have to concede.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing the U.S. market for goods made by children under 15 — is real and the costs are modest: compliance paperwork for importers and slightly higher prices for consumers, weighed against penalties aimed only at goods from identified child-labor industries. The design has weaknesses, notably its reliance on government identification of specific foreign industries rather than banning all child-labor goods outright, and the risk that a ban displaces children into unregulated work. Still, weighed honestly, the human benefit would have outweighed the compliance cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 1992 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which sent it to its Trade Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 1993 — no markup, no floor vote, no further action.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Pease introduced the bill on October 1, 1992 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
On October 6, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Trade, and no further action appears in the record before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Importers and retailers of goods that might contain child labor kept unrestricted access to the U.S. market, and nothing changed for children working in export industries.

for.name: Rep. Donald J. Pease
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Dan Rostenkowski, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Trade Subcommittee and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition cannot be read from the record.

industries.industry: Importers and retailers of labor-intensive consumer goods
industries.note: The bill would have barred entry of goods from identified child-labor industries unless importers certified their supply chains, exposing them to seizures and fines up to $25,000 per violation. Its death left their sourcing practices untouched.

industries.industry: U.S. manufacturers competing with low-wage imports
industries.note: The bill's findings argued U.S. workers should not face jobs imperiled by imports made with child labor, so domestic producers would have faced less competition from goods produced at near-zero labor cost.

industries.industry: Foreign export industries using child labor
industries.note: Identified industries would have lost the U.S. market for their products. The bill aimed to price child labor out of export production and push those economies toward adult employment and schooling.
